clue.text: Insubstantial wages, limiting for each

indicators.note: to limit something is to hem it in, so the wages enclose the other piece

parts.note: pay is what you earn
per means for each, as in 'ten pounds per head'

explanation.surface: A complaint that wages are pitiful even when reckoned person by person.
explanation.definitionFit: Something papery is thin and flimsy like paper, hence lacking substance.

clue.text: Proper media work exists, e.g. knocking out article

indicators.note: knocking something out removes it, so the article's letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: PR, public relations, is work dealing with the media
is means exists, as in 'there is'
say introduces an example, as e.g. does
a is the indefinite article, here removed

explanation.surface: A note that proper media work exists, giving an example by cutting an article.
explanation.walkthrough: SAY loses its A to give SY.
explanation.definitionFit: Prissy describes someone fussily prim and correct, an overly proper manner.

clue.text: Sausage: energy needed by individual dispatching second one

indicators.note: dispatching means getting rid of, and second refers to a letter position, so the second letter of the next word goes

parts.note: pep is energy or vigour
a person is an individual
one as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A butcher's note: making this sausage takes effort from someone who discards the second one.
explanation.walkthrough: PERSON loses its second S to give PERON.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepperoni is a spicy Italian-American dry sausage, often sliced onto pizza.

clue.text: Government area yielding nothing for me

indicators.note: to yield is to give way, so one piece gives up its place and another stands in

parts.note: a region is an area
o looks like zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A local official complains that a government area gives nothing back to them.
explanation.walkthrough: In REGION the O is swapped for ME. 'For' here means 'in exchange for'.
explanation.definitionFit: Regimen in an older sense means a system of government or rule, related to regime.

clue.text: State, very American? Two, encompassing Connecticut and Oregon, included in that

indicators.note: to encompass is to surround, so the pair of ones goes round the two state abbreviations
'that' points back to the first pair of pieces, which takes the middle group inside it

parts.note: v is the standard abbreviation for very
two in Roman numerals, here split to go either side
the US postal code for Connecticut
the US postal code for Oregon
A is a standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A puzzle about US states and their abbreviations, as if asking which state is very American.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at American states and postal codes, but the answer is an Australian state; 'that' refers back to the very-American pair, which holds everything else.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria is one of the six states of Australia, with Melbourne as its capital.

clue.text: Cocktail of gin? Grudgingly dispenses volume with skill

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written for the mix

indicators.note: to dispense with something is to do without it, so the abbreviation is removed

parts.note: to grant something grudgingly is to do it enviously
v is the abbreviation for volume

explanation.surface: Someone serves a gin cocktail reluctantly, yet measures it out skilfully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grudgingly' is not a deletion signal but a word to translate; only after translating it does the volume abbreviation come out.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something ingeniously is to do it cleverly and inventively, with skill.

clue.text: Type of holiday company to take in a bird in Africa

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so the company abbreviation surrounds the article

parts.note: a tour is a kind of holiday
Co is the abbreviation for company
taken as written

explanation.surface: A travel firm offers holidays to see birds in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: TOUR then C(A)O.
explanation.definitionFit: The touraco, or turaco, is a brightly coloured fruit-eating bird found only in sub-Saharan Africa.

clue.text: Bits of uneven ground — not good — trips up?

indicators.note: not means without here, so the letter for good is left out

parts.note: ridges are raised strips of ground
g is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Uneven ground that isn't good makes people stumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trips up' reads as stumbling, but it means outings taken up on a horse or vehicle; the question mark flags that twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Rides are journeys on horseback or in a vehicle, where the rider is up in the saddle or seat.

clue.text: It's drunk and it's eaten at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written for the shuffle

explanation.surface: A seasick passenger reports that whatever is consumed on board, food or drink, comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's drunk' sounds like a tipsy person, but it means a thing that is drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Anisette is an aniseed-flavoured liqueur, so it is a drink.

clue.text: Criticise the writer's joke about golf

parts.note: the writer of the clue saying 'I am', contracted to I'm

indicators.note: about means around here, so the joke is wrapped round the abbreviation for the sport

parts.note: a pun is a joke on words
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An author's jokey remark about golf draws criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: I'M followed by PU(G)N.
explanation.definitionFit: To impugn is to dispute or attack the truth or honesty of something, a formal synonym of criticise.

clue.text: I'd performed in choir, retaining energy, returning after a part of the Mass

parts.note: taken as written; the rest comes after it

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the combined string is read from right to left
to retain is to hold on to, so the first word keeps the energy symbol inside it

parts.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy
a choir's performance is sung

explanation.surface: A chorister proudly recalls singing in a choir, and the context of church music fits a Mass.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the I'd-plus-sung string turns round; the lone 'a' stays put at the front, as 'after a' places the turned string behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Agnus Dei, 'Lamb of God', is the prayer sung near the end of the Latin Mass, a section in musical settings.

clue.text: Pressing item: closure of outrageous couple of clubs

indicators.note: the closure of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of outrageous
two kinds of club: a TEAM is a sports club and an IRON is a golf club

explanation.surface: A golfer or club secretary complains that two clubs have been outrageously shut down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' means two different things: a football-style club gives TEAM, and a golf club gives IRON.
explanation.definitionFit: A steam iron is a domestic appliance for pressing clothes, so it is literally an item used for pressing.

clue.text: Soldiers agree to restrict crisis in later engagement

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so the soldiers and agreement together enclose the crisis

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a turn can mean a crisis or turning point, as in an illness taking a turn
things that match agree with each other

explanation.surface: Troops agree to contain a crisis before a later battle.
explanation.walkthrough: The soldiers and the agreeing word together form the outer shell, with the crisis sitting at their join.
explanation.definitionFit: A return match is a second game between the same opponents, a later engagement in the sporting sense.

clue.text: Area of supermarket is covered in beer

indicators.note: something covered in a liquid is surrounded by it, so the beer goes round the short word

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spilled drink leaves part of the supermarket swimming in beer.
explanation.walkthrough: A(IS)LE.
explanation.definitionFit: An aisle is a walkway between shelves in a shop, one of the areas shoppers move through.

clue.text: Who'd be excited by latest glimpse of owl or its hooting?

definitions.text: Who'd be excited by latest glimpse of owl or its hooting?

indicators.note: excited letters are agitated and stirred up, so they are rearranged
the latest part of a word to be seen is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the last letter of owl
taken as written for the shuffle

explanation.surface: A wry question: what sort of person gets thrilled by a fleeting sight of an owl or the sound of its hoot?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a birdwatcher would indeed be excited by seeing or hearing an owl.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornithologist studies birds, so a glimpse or call of an owl is exactly what excites such a scientist.

clue.text: Idea from Paris about record held by Oxford University dogmatist

indicators.note: about means around, so the French word surrounds the rest

parts.note: idee is French for idea

indicators.note: something held by another sits inside it, so the record goes inside the university's initials

parts.note: OU, the initials of Oxford University
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: A French notion, recorded in an Oxford archive, belongs to a rigid thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From Paris' signals a French word; the French for idea is spelt with two Es, which split to hold the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideologue is someone rigidly committed to a doctrine, hence a dogmatic person.

clue.text: Help to secure stone and mineral turning up in orbiting body

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, here by enclosing it

parts.note: aid is help
st is the abbreviation for stone, a British unit of weight

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means reading upwards, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: ore is mineral-bearing rock

explanation.surface: A rescue effort to secure stone and minerals unearthed in a spacecraft.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of weight, 14 pounds, abbreviated st.
explanation.definitionFit: An asteroid is a small rocky body orbiting the sun, mostly between Mars and Jupiter.

clue.text: Worsening situation a must for 24 events?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a course of events that leads step by step to something worse
second meaning, taken literally: an icy ski slope, essential for skiing away from groomed runs

explanation.walkthrough: 24 is OFF-PISTE, skiing outside marked runs; read literally, the answer is a slope that is slippery, which such skiing needs. The question mark flags this playful second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a process where one small step leads inevitably to worse ones, while the literal phrase describes snowy terrain for skiers.

clue.text: Composer raised trophy: first in competition in Italy

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means lifted upward, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a cup is a trophy

indicators.note: the first in a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the first letter of competition
taken as written
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A football report: a cup raised by the winner of a competition in Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Giacomo Puccini was the Italian composer of operas such as La Bohème and Tosca.

clue.text: Energy in poorly stored magnetic field is measured by this

definitions.text: magnetic field is measured by this

indicators.note: something poorly arranged is in bad order, so the letters need sorting out

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
taken as written for the shuffle

explanation.surface: A physics remark about energy held badly in a magnetic field and how to gauge it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a physics statement; the answer is the unit, named after Hans Christian Ørsted.
explanation.definitionFit: The oersted is the CGS unit of magnetic field strength, so it is what such a field is measured in.

clue.text: Turn mouldy at last in jar

indicators.note: in places the selected letter inside the other word

parts.note: to jar and to grate both mean to irritate or sound harshly

indicators.note: at last points to the end of the word, so only its final letter is used

parts.note: the last letter of mouldy

explanation.surface: Food in a jar has finally turned mouldy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' and 'jar' look like a food-going-off scene, but jar is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To gyrate is to rotate or spin round, so to turn.

clue.text: System of behaviour and so forth limiting welcome

indicators.note: to limit something is to hem it in on both sides, so the first piece encloses the greeting

parts.note: etc, et cetera, means and so forth
hi is a word of welcome

explanation.surface: A list of manners and so forth that might restrict how warmly guests are greeted.
explanation.walkthrough: ET(HI)C.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethic is a set of moral principles governing conduct, such as a work ethic.

clue.text: Substantial expression of surprise about newspaper

indicators.note: about means around, so the exclamation wraps round the newspaper's initials

parts.note: hey is an exclamation
FT, the Financial Times, a British newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise at a weighty newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: HE(FT)Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Hefty means large and heavy, a synonym of substantial.

clue.text: Decent standards I abandoned accepting a year in council office

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the shortened word takes the other letters inside it
the letter said to be abandoned is left out of the word for standards

parts.note: morality is a code of decent standards
the letter to remove
taken as written
y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A councillor laments that decent standards were dropped within a year of taking office.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for decent standards has two Is; it is the second that goes.
explanation.definitionFit: The mayoralty is the office or term of a mayor, the head of a town or city council.

clue.text: Son invested in mine, blocking most of proposal not following standard route

indicators.note: money invested in something goes inside it, so the son's letter is put inside the mine
most of a word means all but its last letter, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: an offer is a proposal

indicators.note: something blocking a passage sits in the middle of it, so this combined piece sits inside the shortened proposal

parts.note: a pit is a mine, such as a coal pit
s is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A family dispute where a son puts money into a mine and so thwarts a takeover bid.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: the son goes into the mine, then that unit goes inside the shortened proposal.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-piste skiing goes away from the prepared runs, and by extension it means departing from the usual way.

clue.text: Character from Greece concealing source of this mark of disgrace

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so the Greek letter wraps round the single letter

parts.note: sigma is a letter of the Greek alphabet

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it starts, so its first letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of this

explanation.surface: A Greek letter being used to hide a shameful mark, like a tattoo.
explanation.walkthrough: S(T)IGMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a mark of shame attached to a person or circumstance, originally a brand on the skin.

clue.text: Clear space is not needed by flower without much substance

indicators.note: the short word is said to be unwanted, so it is taken out of the flower's name

parts.note: a daisy is a common flower
taken as written, to be removed
light means insubstantial, lacking weight

explanation.surface: A gardener remarks that a flimsy flower doesn't need open space around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' is both a clue word and the letters dropped from the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Daylight can mean a visible gap or clear distance between things, as in 'there's daylight between the two runners'.

clue.text: A Democrat now to remain faithful

parts.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for a US Democrat
here can mean at this point in time, as in 'here we go'

explanation.surface: A politician switches party and now pledges loyalty as a Democrat.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere to a cause or belief is to stick with it loyally, a synonym of staying faithful.
